steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our computational geometry paper on choosing a minimum set of plane obstacles that encloses all given points. Place it among related obstacle problems, define the problem, sketch our two approximation frameworks, and include a related-work subsection on point separation and obstacle removal.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Plane obstacle problems in computational geometry
2. The Enclosing-All-Points problem
3. Relation to (generalized) point separation; novelty
4. Our two frameworks: sparsification + min-cut; LP rounding
5. Related work: point separation; obstacle removal

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Plane obstacles
- given geometric objects in the plane as obstacles; an obstacle blocks all paths it intersects
- shortest paths between two points amidst obstacles
- obstacle-removal: min subset to remove so two points get connected
- point-separation: min subset separating a point set X (block all paths between two points in X)

2. Enclosing-All-Points
- x enclosed by \mathcal{O} if x lies in a bounded connected component of \mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash(\bigcup_{O\in\mathcal{O}}O)
- i.e. any curve from x to (+\infty,0) hits some object; Figure 1
- goal: minimum subset of obstacles enclosing all input points

3. Relation to point separation
- special case of generalized point-separation from Kumar et al.: separate point-pairs \{(s_{1},t_{1}),\dots,(s_{r},t_{r})\}, i\in[r]
- enclose X = separate \{(x,z):x\in X\} with z=(+\infty,0)
- Kumar et al.: polynomial when number of pairs fixed, any connected obstacles
- doesn't solve our problem: X part of input; no nontrivial algorithms known when number of pairs not fixed
- not studied before

## Sparsification and min-cut
- step 1: sparse subset \mathcal{O}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{O}, optimal solution on it is O(1) -approximation; sparse = any point stabs O(1) obstacles
- step 2: reduce to min-cut in a graph (polynomial), constant factor loss
- O(1) -approximation for similarly-sized fat pseudo-disks (unit-disks, unit squares)

## LP rounding
- more general obstacles, worse ratios
- line segments: O(\alpha(n)\log n) -approximation (\alpha(n) inverse Ackermann)
- general disks: O(\log n)
- curves pairwise intersecting s=O(1) times: \alpha(n)^{O(\alpha(n)^{s-1})}\log n
- applying LP rounding non-obvious; new ideas in both LP formulation and rounding

## Related work
- not studied before; summarize point-separation and obstacle-removal

## Point separation
- X, \mathcal{O} in \mathbb{R}^{2}; minimum \mathcal{O}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{O} separating all points in X; barrier coverage with wireless sensors
- Gibson et al.: NP-hard for unit disks (from planar multiterminal-cut); (9+\varepsilon) -approximation for general disks
- Cabello and Giannopoulos: first poly exact algorithm for arbitrary connected curves, |X|=2, O(n^{3}) time; NP-hard with unit circles or orthogonal segments (planar-3-SAT)
- Kumar et al.: generalize to n^{O(|X|)} time

## Obstacle removal
- s,t; minimum \mathcal{O}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{O} s.t. s and t not separated by \mathcal{O}\backslash\mathcal{O}^{*}
- a.k.a. barrier resilience: min sensors to deactivate for a path avoiding active sensors; robotics applications
- NP-hard: arbitrary line segments; unit segments; fat regions with bounded ply (axis-aligned rectangles of aspect ratio 1:1+\varepsilon and 1+\varepsilon:1)
- Bereg and Kirkpatrick: 3 -approximation for unit disks
- Bandyapadhyay et al.: O(\sqrt{n}) -approximation, pseudodisks and rectilinear polygons
- Kumar et al.: O(1) -approximation for well-behaved objects (polygons, splines); later simplified

steps.text:
Problems related to plane obstacles are a popular topic in computational geometry. In the usual setting of these problems, we are given a set of geometric objects in the plane as obstacles, and an obstacle blocks all paths in the plane that it intersects. Many optimization problems have been studied in this setting. For example, one line of research is about finding shortest paths between two points amidst the given obstacles. The obstacle-removal problem asks for a minimum subset of obstacles such that after removing them, two specified points in the plane have a path between them. The point-separation problem wants to select a minimum subset of obstacles that separate a given set X of points, i.e., block all paths between two points in X.

In this paper we study a natural problem related to plane obstacles, which we call Enclosing-All-Points. A point x in the plane is enclosed by a set \mathcal{O} of (compact) geometric objects if x lies in a bounded connected component of \mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash(\bigcup_{O\in\mathcal{O}}O). In other words, any curve that connects x with the point (+\infty,0) at infinity has to intersect at least one object in \mathcal{O}. Figure 1 shows an example. The problem is to compute a minimum subset of obstacles that encloses all the input points.

Enclosing-All-Points is closely related to the point-separation problem mentioned above. Actually, it is a special case of the generalized point-separation problem studied in, where we want to use a minimum number of obstacles to separate a set of point-pairs \{(s_{1},t_{1}),\dots,(s_{r},t_{r})\} in the plane, i.e., block all paths between s_{i} and t_{i} for all i\in[r]. Enclosing a point-set X is the same as separating the point-pairs in \{(x,z):x\in X\}, where z=(+\infty,0) is the point at infinity. Kumar et al. showed that the generalized point-separation problem is polynomial-time solvable for any connected obstacles when the number of point-pairs to separate is fixed. But this does not solve Enclosing-All-Points, because in our problem the set X is part of the input, and when the number of point-pairs is not fixed no nontrivial algorithms for generalized point-separation were known. As far as we know, Enclosing-All-Points has not been studied before.

- curves pairwise intersecting s=O(1) times: \alpha(n)^{O(\alpha(n)^{s-1})}\log n
- applying LP rounding non-obvious; new ideas in both LP formulation and rounding

- not studied before; summarize point-separation and obstacle-removal

- Kumar et al.: generalize to n^{O(|X|)} time

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Problems related to plane obstacles are a popular topic in computational geometry. In the usual setting of these problems, we are given a set of geometric objects in the plane as obstacles, and an obstacle blocks all paths in the plane that it intersects. Many optimization problems have been studied in this setting. For example, one line of research is about finding shortest paths between two points amidst the given obstacles. The obstacle-removal problem asks for a minimum subset of obstacles such that after removing them, two specified points in the plane have a path between them. The point-separation problem wants to select a minimum subset of obstacles that separate a given set X of points, i.e., block all paths between two points in X.

In this paper we study a natural problem related to plane obstacles, which we call Enclosing-All-Points. A point x in the plane is enclosed by a set \mathcal{O} of (compact) geometric objects if x lies in a bounded connected component of \mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash(\bigcup_{O\in\mathcal{O}}O). In other words, any curve that connects x with the point (+\infty,0) at infinity has to intersect at least one object in \mathcal{O}. Figure 1 shows an example. The problem is to compute a minimum subset of obstacles that encloses all the input points.

Enclosing-All-Points is closely related to the point-separation problem mentioned above. Actually, it is a special case of the generalized point-separation problem studied in, where we want to use a minimum number of obstacles to separate a set of point-pairs \{(s_{1},t_{1}),\dots,(s_{r},t_{r})\} in the plane, i.e., block all paths between s_{i} and t_{i} for all i\in[r]. Enclosing a point-set X is the same as separating the point-pairs in \{(x,z):x\in X\}, where z=(+\infty,0) is the point at infinity. Kumar et al. showed that the generalized point-separation problem is polynomial-time solvable for any connected obstacles when the number of point-pairs to separate is fixed. But this does not solve Enclosing-All-Points, because in our problem the set X is part of the input, and when the number of point-pairs is not fixed no nontrivial algorithms for generalized point-separation were known. As far as we know, Enclosing-All-Points has not been studied before.

In this paper we propose two general algorithmic frameworks for designing polynomial-time approximation algorithms for Enclosing-All-Points.

## Approach based on sparsification and min-cut.

The first framework solves Enclosing-All-Points in two steps. The first step computes a sparse subset \mathcal{O}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{O} of obstacles such that an optimal solution using the obstacles in \mathcal{O}^{\prime} is an O(1) -approximation solution of the original problem for \mathcal{O}. Here "sparse" roughly means that any point in the plane stabs O(1) obstacles in \mathcal{O}^{\prime}. The second step reduces the problem on \mathcal{O}^{\prime} to a min-cut problem in a graph, which is polynomial-time solvable, and loses a constant factor in the cost. This framework gives O(1) -approximation algorithms for the problem with similarly-sized fat pseudo-disks, e.g., unit-disks, unit squares, etc.

## Approach based on LP rounding.

The second framework uses LP rounding. It applies to more general types of obstacles than the first one, but the approximation ratios are worse. It gives an O(\alpha(n)\log n) -approximation algorithm for Enclosing-All-Points with line segments, where \alpha(n) is the inverse Ackermann function, and an O(\log n) -approximation algorithm for Enclosing-All-Points with (general) disks. The framework also generalizes to the problem with curves that pairwise intersect s=O(1) times, with approximation ratio \alpha(n)^{O(\alpha(n)^{s-1})}\log n. LP rounding is a common technique used widely for designing approximation algorithms, but how to use it for Enclosing-All-Points is not obvious at all. For our problem we need new ideas in both the LP formulation and the rounding scheme.

## 1.1 Related work

As far as we know, Enclosing-All-Points has not been studied before. Here we briefly summarize the literature for two problems closely related to it, the point-separation problem and the obstacle-removal problem.

## Point separation.

Given a set X of points and a set \mathcal{O} of obstacles in \mathbb{R}^{2}, the point-separation problem asks for a minimum subset \mathcal{O}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{O} that separates all points in X. The problem has applications in barrier coverage with wireless sensors. Gibson et al. showed the problem is NP-hard for unit disks by a reduction from planar multiterminal-cut, and gave an (9+\varepsilon) -approximation algorithm that works for (general) disks. Then Cabello and Giannopoulos designed the first polynomial-time exact algorithm for point-separation with arbitrary connected curves for the case |X|=2, which runs in O(n^{3}) time. They also showed the problem is NP-hard with unit circles or orthogonal segments, by a reduction from planar-3-SAT. Recently Kumar et al. generalized the algorithm of Cabello and Giannopoulos and showed that point-separation with arbitrary connected curves can be solved in n^{O(|X|)} time.

## Obstacle removal.

Given two points s,t and a set \mathcal{O} of obstacles in \mathbb{R}^{2}, the obstacle problem asks for a minimum subset \mathcal{O}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{O} such that s and t are not separated by \mathcal{O}\backslash\mathcal{O}^{*}. This problem is sometimes also called computing the barrier resilience. A real-world application is to compute the minimum number of sensors that have to be deactivated so that there is a path between s and t that does not intersect any active sensor. It also has applications in robotics. Obstacle-removal was shown to be NP-hard for arbitrary line segments, for unit segments, and for certain types of fat regions with bounded ply (such as axis-aligned rectangles of aspect ratio 1:1+\varepsilon and 1+\varepsilon:1). On the approximation side, Bereg and Kirkpatrick gave a 3 -approximation algorithm for unit disks. Bandyapadhyay et al. gave an O(\sqrt{n}) -approximation algorithm for pseudodisks and rectilinear polygons. Kumar et al. then designed an O(1) -approximation algorithm for any well-behaved objects, such as polygons or splines. Their arguments were simplified later by Kumar et al..

steps.text:
Problems related to plane obstacles are a popular topic in computational geometry. In the common setting of such problems, we are given a set of geometric objects in the plane as obstacles. An obstacle blocks all paths in the plane it intersects. Various optimization problems have been investigated in this setting. For example, a line of research [1,2,3,4,5,6] focused on finding shortest paths between two points amidst the given obstacles. The obstacle-removal problem [7,8,9,10] asks for a minimum subset of obstacles such that after removing these obstacles, two specified points in the plane have a path between them. The point-separation problem [11,12,9] aims to select a minimum subset of obstacles that separate a given set X of points, i.e., block all paths between two points in X.

In this paper, we study a natural problem related to plane obstacles, which we call Enclosing-All-Points. We say a point x in the plane is enclosed by a set \mathcal{O} of (compact) geometric objects if x lies in a bounded connected component of \mathbb{R}^{2}\backslash(\bigcup_{O\in\mathcal{O}}O); in other words, any curve connecting x with the point (+\infty,0) at infinity must intersect with at least one object in \mathcal{O}. An example is shown in Figure 1. The problem aims to compute a minimum subset of obstacles to enclose all input points.

Enclosing-All-Points is closely related to the aforementioned point-separation problem. Actually, it is a special case of the generalized point-separation problem studied in [9], in which we want to use a minimum number of obstacles to separate a set of point-pairs \{(s_{1},t_{1}),\dots,(s_{r},t_{r})\} in the plane, i.e., block all paths between s_{i} and t_{i} for all i\in[r]. Enclosing a point-set X is equivalent to separating the point-pairs in \{(x,z):x\in X\}, where z=(+\infty,0) is the point at infinity. Kumar et al. [9] showed that when the number of point-pairs to be separated is fixed, the generalized point-separation problem is polynomial-time solvable for any connected obstacles. However, this does not solve the Enclosing-All-Points problem, since in our problem the set X is a part of the input (when the number of point-pairs is not fixed, no nontrivial algorithms for the generalized point-separation problem were known). To the best of our knowledge, Enclosing-All-Points has not been studied before.

In this paper, we propose two general algorithmic frameworks to design polynomial-time approximation algorithms for Enclosing-All-Points.

## Approach based on sparsification and min-cut.

Our first framework solves Enclosing-All-Points via two steps. The first step computes a sparse subset \mathcal{O}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{O} of obstacles such that an optimal solution using the obstacles in \mathcal{O}^{\prime} is an O(1) -approximation solution of the original problem for \mathcal{O}. Here “sparse” roughly means that any point in the plane stabs O(1) obstacles in \mathcal{O}^{\prime}. The second step reduces the problem on \mathcal{O}^{\prime} to a min-cut problem in a graph (which is polynomial-time solvable) by losing a constant factor in cost. This framework results in O(1) -approximation algorithms for the problem with similarly-sized fat pseudo-disks, e.g., unit-disks, unit squares, etc.

## Approach based on LP rounding.

Our second framework is based on LP rounding. Compared to the first one, this framework applies to more general types of obstacles, while giving worse approximation ratios. Specifically, it results in an O(\alpha(n)\log n) -approximation algorithm for Enclosing-All-Points with line segments, where \alpha(n) denotes the inverse Ackermann function, and an O(\log n) -approximation algorithm for Enclosing-All-Points with (general) disks. The framework also generalizes to the problem with curves that pairwise intersect s=O(1) times, with an approximation ratio \alpha(n)^{O(\alpha(n)^{s-1})}\log n. Although LP rounding is a common technique widely used for designing approximation algorithms, how to apply it for Enclosing-All-Points is not obvious at all. In fact, for our problem, new ideas are required in both the LP formulation and the rounding scheme.

## 1.1 Related work

To the best of our knowledge, Enclosing-All-Points has not been studied before. Here we briefly summarize the literature for two problems that are closely related to Enclosing-All-Points, the point-separation problem and the obstacle-removal problem.

## Point separation.

Given a set X of points and a set \mathcal{O} of obstacles in \mathbb{R}^{2}, the point-separation problem asks for a minimum subset \mathcal{O}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{O} that separates all points in X. This problem has applications in barrier coverage with wireless sensors. Gibson et al. [12] showed the NP-hardness of the problem for unit disks by reducing from planar multiterminal-cut, and presented an (9+\varepsilon) -approximation algorithm that works for (general) disks. Then, Cabello and Giannopoulos [11] designed the first polynomial-time exact algorithm for point-separation with arbitrary connected curves for the case |X|=2, which runs in O(n^{3}) time. They also showed NP-hardness of the problem with unit circles or orthogonal segments, via a reduction from planar-3-SAT. Recently, Kumar et al. [9] generalizes the algorithm of Cabello and Giannopoulos [11] and showed that point-separation with arbitrary connected curves can be solved in n^{O(|X|)} time.

## Obstacle removal.

Given two points s,t and a set \mathcal{O} of obstacles in \mathbb{R}^{2}, the obstacle problem asks for a minimum subset \mathcal{O}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{O} such that s and t are not separated by \mathcal{O}\backslash\mathcal{O}^{*}. This problem is also sometimes called computing the barrier resilience [7,10], where a real-world application is to compute the minimum number of sensors that need to be deactivated, so that there is a path between s and t that does not intersect any of the active sensors. It also has applications in robotics [13,14]. Obstacle-removal was shown to be NP-hard for arbitrary line segments [15], for unit segments [16,17], and for certain types of fat regions with bounded ply (such as axis-aligned rectangles of aspect ratio 1:1+\varepsilon and 1+\varepsilon:1) [18]. For approximation results, Bereg and Kirkpatrick provided a 3 -approximation algorithm for unit disks [19]. Bandyapadhyay et al. [20] presented an O(\sqrt{n}) -approximation algorithm for pseudodisks and rectilinear polygons. Kumar et al. [8] then designed an O(1) -approximation algorithm for any well-behaved objects, such as polygons or splines. Their arguments were later simplified by Kumar et al. [9].
